segments: 3 Stoic rules for overthinkers.

1. Ask: is this up to me?
If not, it isn’t yours to carry.

2. Name the worst case.
Seneca did. It’s usually survivable.

3. Do the next small thing.
Thought ends where action starts.
Save this for the next 2am spiral.

The fastest way to lose an argument?
Get angry.
Marcus Aurelius wrote this down:

“How much more grievous are
the consequences of anger
than the causes of it.”
Pause. Breathe. Answer later.

Whoever stays calm
stays in control.

Send this to someone
with a short fuse.
You’re acting like you have forever.
Marcus Aurelius reminded himself:

“You could leave life right now.
Let that determine what you do
and say and think.”

Not to scare you.
To wake you up.
What are you still postponing?
Follow for one Stoic rule a day.
You can’t make everyone like you.
Epictetus told his students:

“If you want to improve,
be content to be thought
foolish and stupid.”
Their approval isn’t the goal.
Your character is.
Send this to a people pleaser.
The thing blocking your path?
That is the path.

“The impediment to action
advances action. What stands
in the way becomes the way.”
Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 5.20

Every setback is training.
Use it.
Save this for your next bad day.

Busy all day.
Nothing done.
Seneca saw this 2,000 years ago.

“It is not that we have
a short time to live, but
that we waste a lot of it.”
You guard your money.
Guard your hours harder.
Follow for more Stoic rules.
5 things you can’t control:

What they think of you.
The past. Other people’s choices.
The weather. The outcome.
5 things you can:

Your effort. Your words.
Your response. Your habits.
Your attention.

Epictetus:
“Some things are up to us,
and some are not.”
Save this.
Not every insult deserves a reply.
Marcus Aurelius had a better idea.

“The best revenge is to be unlike
him who performed the injury.”
Silence isn’t weakness.
It’s control.
Send this to someone who needs it.
Stop counting what you don’t have.
Marcus Aurelius:

“Think not so much
of what you lack
as of what you have.”

Picture losing it all.
Then look again.
You’re richer than you think.
Follow for one Stoic rule a day.
Motivation isn’t coming.

Marcus Aurelius didn’t want
to get out of bed either.

“At dawn, when you have
trouble getting out of bed,
tell yourself: I have to go
to work, as a human being.”
He didn’t wait to feel ready.
Neither should you.
Save this for tomorrow morning.
It’s not what happened that hurts.
It’s the story you tell about it.

“Choose not to be harmed,
and you won’t feel harmed.”
Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 4.7

Change the story.
Change the feeling.

Send this to someone
hurting today.
Lost something you loved?
Epictetus offered one sentence.

“Never say of anything,
‘I have lost it’; but,
‘I have returned it.’”

Nothing was ever really ours.
It was lent.
Be grateful you had it.
Follow for more Stoic rules.
Look at your five closest friends.
That’s who you’re becoming.
Seneca to Lucilius:

“Associate with those who will
make a better man of you.”
Choose your circle on purpose.

Tag the friend who
makes you better.
You keep living in yesterday.
Or worrying about tomorrow.

“Each of us lives only now,
this brief instant.
The rest has been lived already.”
Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 3.10
This is the only moment you get.
Save this for when you drift.
